name: PT Ifishdeco Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ifishdeco: a short ore life, a thin float and a price that already discounts recovery
frontmatter.summary: IFSH is a small Indonesian nickel-ore producer. We value the ore with a life-of-asset DCF, deduct the minorities at economic value rather than at book, and apply the konglo lens to a register with a fraction of a per cent in public hands. The shares already price nickel above the house marker, so we start at HOLD with a target close to the market price and a failed liquidity screen.
thesis: The primary method is a life-of-asset DCF. The approved nickel-ore plan is held flat to the national reserve horizon, then the mine stops, with no terminal value. After the minority is deducted at its economic share the DCF is Rp699 a share and the weighted value is Rp774 [S0, S7].

The market is ahead of that. At Rp805 the stock is 1.39x the fundamental value today of Rp579, and the reverse DCF needs nickel at US$18,628.2 a tonne — above the through-cycle marker of US$17,500.0 and above the spot print of US$16,324.0.

The float is the regime. With 0.48 per cent in public hands, HSC status and a 14.5% gap to the minimum by 31 March 2029, the konglo lens keeps part of the premium rather than closing it, which is why the target (Rp774) sits above fundamental value and below the price.
The cushion is thinner than the balance sheet suggests — net debt of IDR-70.6bn (negative is net cash) after a working-capital build, with a 4.1% yield at the current price [S0].

The ore life beyond the national sub-ten-year statement is unknown, and we say so rather than invent a number; exploration is paid for and not credited. The bull case is the approved 2,200 kt kt RKAB plus a signed acquisition [S16].
The name fails the house liquidity screen — average daily value of IDR291.8m — so it is a monitor-only position, not an actionable one [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Ifishdeco Tbk with a **HOLD** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp774**, against a price of Rp805 — a total return of 0.3% including the dividend. The target is the output of the house konglo lens, not a stand-alone number: the fundamental twelve-month value after the float and liquidity discounts is Rp619, the pre-discount weighted method value is Rp774, and the lens keeps part of the gap between price and value because a free-float register of 0.48 per cent does not reprice to fundamentals on a twelve-month clock [S0, konglo registry].

Two things changed in this revision, and both are disclosed because they moved the number. The first is the minority interest. The DCF discounts the whole group's free cash flow, so the minority's claim has to come out at value, not at the book carrying amount: minorities took IDR34.4bn of the IDR106.5bn group profit in FY2025, and at that share the deduction is several times the book minority the model previously used, so it is now carried as a bridge item below the DCF [S0]. The second is the base year. The first half of FY2026 is an actual, not a forecast, and our FY2026E revenue is now set on it rather than on a second-half step-up the record does not support [S5].

The business is simple to describe and hard to value richly. IFSH mines nickel ore and silica sand from a 800 ha ha IUP Operation/Production area inside a 2,580 ha ha concession in Tinanggea, South Konawe, Southeast Sulawesi, and sells the ore to Indonesian smelters; a subsidiary holds nickel-pig-iron and ferronickel processing assets [S11, S12]. In FY2025 it sold 1,290 kt kt of nickel ore and 978 kt kt of silica, earned IDR1,000.0bn of revenue and IDR106.5bn of group net profit [S2]. The first half of FY2026 was much stronger — net sales of IDR634.3bn and net profit of IDR46.2bn, a swing from loss [S5] — but we will not extrapolate a margin we cannot decompose from the half-year lines the record carries, which is why the full year is set at the annualised half with no second-half step-up [S5].

The variant view is about the ore body and the equity bridge, not the nickel price. Our base case holds the company's approved 1,490 kt kt sales plan flat to the national reserve horizon and then stops — a ten-year placeholder taken from the Directorate General of Mineral and Coal's statement that the national saprolite reserve life is under ten years, because no company reserve, resource or IUP-expiry figure could be sourced, and the scenarios re-cut the life both ways [S7, S16]. A life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value gives Rp699 a share. The cross-checks bracket it: EV/EBITDA at 7.5x gives Rp690 and book value at 1.1x gives Rp496. The weighted value before the discounts is Rp774; the float and liquidity discounts take it to Rp619 [S0].

What the market is paying for is visible in the reverse DCF. Today's price implies a nickel price of US$18,628.2 a tonne. That is above the house deck's through-cycle marker of US$17,500.0, and the marker is itself above the spot print of US$16,324.0 — so the shares are not discounting a nickel bust, they are discounting a nickel price above the deck's own long-run view. With the through-cycle marker where it is, the value we can defend is below the price [S7].

The cushion is thinner than the FY2025 balance sheet suggests. The group still carries net cash — net debt of IDR-70.6bn on our numbers, where negative is net cash — but the FY2025 working-capital build at a 22.9% ratio absorbs most of the operating cash, and the market capitalisation is IDR1,548.3bn [S0]. A payout of 69.3% of parent earnings supports a 4.1% yield at the current price — modest, and it is what turns a -3.8% price downside into a total return of 0.3%; it is not a reason to own the name.

Two disclosures complete the picture. The engine's investability screen fails on turnover: average daily value is IDR291.8m against the house floor for Indonesian equities, while market capitalisation passes [S0]. A position that matters could not be built or exited at that turnover, and the 20.0% liquidity discount in the valuation is the price of it. The name is therefore monitor-only for the desk until turnover improves, whatever the rating says.

A small-cap Indonesian miner with a concentrated shareholder register behaves differently from
a large, liquid producer. The controlling family and affiliates hold most of the shares, a
thin sliver trades, and index inclusion or exclusion can move the price more than a quarter of
earnings. That is the regime this name sits in, and it is why the report separates the
fundamental value of the ore from the price the float sets.

The three things that move the value are, in order: the nickel price relative to the through-cycle marker; the volume and life of the ore body, including whether the mooted acquisitions are signed and priced; and the permit and governance record, which is where the tail risk sits. We take each in turn below.
What the company does

PT Ifishdeco Tbk was founded in 1971 as a fisheries company, moved into agribusiness plantation in 1989, and found nickel and iron in its plantation ground during soil surveys between 2005 and 2008. It applied for a nickel IUP exploration licence in 2008, upgraded to an IUP Operation/Production in 2010 and began producing and selling nickel ore in 2011 [S11, S16]. The company is therefore a first-generation ore miner that converted a plantation concession into a nickel mine, not a diversified metals group.

The concession is in Tinanggea, South Konawe Regency, Southeast Sulawesi. IFSH holds 2,580 ha ha in total, of which 800 ha ha are covered by the IUP Operation/Production [S11, S12]. The company produces and sells raw ore to smelters operating in Indonesia and manages exploration, infrastructure, production, transport, trading and sales itself [S11]. Its subsidiary, PT Bintang Smelter Indonesia, is responsible for processing, transport and sales of nickel pig iron and ferronickel alloy [S11]; two further subsidiaries, PT Sarana Bumi Minerindo and PT Patrindo Jaya Makmur, sit inside the group structure [S12].
Products, volumes and mix

The revenue base is two ores. In FY2025 IFSH sold 1,290 kt kt of nickel ore, equal to well under its FY2025 RKAB quota of 2,200 kt kt, and 978 kt kt of silica, about two-thirds of the silica RKAB [S2, S16]. Nickel-ore production was 1,670 kt kt, or about three-quarters of the approved RKAB, so the company mined more ore than it sold in FY2025 and carried the difference into the next year [S16]. The FY2026 plan is to sell 1,490 kt kt of nickel ore, in line with the RKAB approved by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources [S16].

The archived record does not give a clean segment revenue split, and the house template carries one priced product. We therefore model nickel-ore tonnes against a blended realisation ratio fitted to total reported revenue, which pulls the silica and any processed-product line into the same revenue base. The financials section explains the arithmetic and what a reader should not read into it: the ratio is a revenue-per-nickel-tonne figure, not an ore price per tonne of nickel metal. It is a documented model limit, not a hidden assumption [S0, S2].
Strategy and capital allocation

Management's stated FY2026 priorities are to optimise the existing IUP under good mining practice, to develop new businesses including coconut planting, and to pursue inorganic growth through mine acquisitions [S2]. On the public-expose call in May 2026 the president director said the company had reviewed four to six candidate mines in Sulawesi and Maluku and that "around half" might be followed up within the year [S16]. The finance director put FY2026 capex at IDR45.0bn, of which the great majority is exploration and a small slice is operating capex [S16]. In our model that plan is carried as capex per tonne; no acquisition is in the base case until a transaction is signed and priced, so the acquisition pipeline is a free option rather than forecast volume.

The dividend is the clearest capital-allocation signal. The FY2026 annual general meeting declared Rp26 a share, IDR50.0bn in total, on FY2025 parent earnings [S2], a payout the company describes as about seven-tenths of net profit. On the group figure that description does not reconcile (IDR50.0bn over IDR106.5bn is well below that), but on parent earnings of IDR72.1bn it does, and parent earnings are the line the dividend is actually paid out of. The company has paid a dividend every year in the data pack's history, with the per-share amount moving with earnings [S0].
Position in the market

IFSH is a price-taker. Its approved annual nickel-ore volume is a rounding error against a national RKAB quota that the ministry revised to 300,000 kt kt for FY2026 [S14, S16], so the company has no influence over the ore price and no scale advantage in bargaining with smelters. Its advantage, such as it is, is location and logistics: the mine sits in the Southeast Sulawesi nickel belt close to domestic smelters, and the ore is sold domestically rather than exported [S11]. Its disadvantage is every small ore seller's — a single mining area, a life that no company statement has quantified, and dependence on the annual RKAB allocation [S7, S12].

Indonesian nickel ore is sold on government reference pricing rather than a freely negotiated
international price, and the annual RKAB work plan and budget is the binding volume control for
every producer. A small miner's economics therefore depend on three things it does not control:
the reference price, the quota it is granted and the smelter's willingness to take its ore. The
company's own operating record — production running below quota in a weak price year — is the
normal pattern for marginal tonnes in this system.
The market and the price

Nickel is the value driver. The house metals deck carries an LME nickel spot of US$16,324/t and a through-cycle marker of US$17,500/t, held flat in real terms thereafter; the FY2026E deck value is US$17,089/t. The deck's long-run marker is a sourced public-series number, not a feeling: the actuals and the forward path come from the World Bank Pink Sheet and the World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook, and the marker sits above the September 2026 spot print. We use that marker for value and treat the spot as cycle position, never as value; the Indonesian reserve arithmetic that supports a through-cycle price above spot is set out below [S7].

The Indonesian supply story is the swing factor. The ministry revised the FY2026 nickel-ore RKAB quota up to 300,000 kt kt from its initial allocation, and the directorate-general has said the national saprolite reserve life is under ten years without more exploration [S14, S7]. Those two statements pull in opposite directions: a larger quota supports more ore supply now, while a short reserve life argues for quota discipline later. The market has been trading the second: press reports in early November 2026 described nickel at a five-week high after Indonesia tightened ore-trading enforcement, and the government has signalled output control through the 2027 RKAB. We do not put a policy number in the model; we let the deck's marker carry the through-cycle view and let the bear and bull cases flex it.
Regulation

Four regulatory layers matter for IFSH. First, the RKAB: annual production and sales quotas are approved by the ministry, and a company can sell less than its quota, as IFSH did in FY2025 [S16]. Second, royalties and reference pricing: ore sales are priced off the government's HMA reference, and the FY2025 average HMA was US$15,177/t a tonne [S2]. Third, forestry and permitting: mining and hauling inside or next to protected forest require a forestry-use approval, and IFSH's own permit history is contested (the governance section). Fourth, export and domestic processing policy: the ore is sold domestically to smelters, so export quotas and the downstreaming rules affect the customer base rather than the company's own export line directly.
Competitive landscape and five forces

The Indonesian nickel-ore industry is fragmented at the mining end and concentrated at the smelting end. The covered peer set — Vale Indonesia, Harita Nickel, Merdeka Battery Materials and Central Omega — spans the range from integrated matte producers to ore sellers, and IFSH belongs at the small, non-integrated end. Its 800 ha ha IUP is tiny against the integrated producers' concessions, and it has no matte or battery-grade nickel capacity of its own [S11, S12].

items: **Supplier power:** moderate. Fuel, tyres, explosives and barging are bought in competitive
markets, but diesel is a large share of a hauling-heavy operation, which is why the model
carries a fuel term tied to the coal index.
**Buyer power:** high. A handful of smelters buy the ore, the product is undifferentiated and
the price is a government reference; a small seller takes the price.
**New entrants:** easy at the mining-licence level, hard at the permit-and-quota level. The
binding constraint is the RKAB allocation and the forestry approval, not geology.
**Substitutes:** low within the nickel chain; the longer-run substitute is battery chemistry
that uses less nickel, a demand-side risk rather than a today risk.
**Rivalry:** high. National ore output runs into the hundreds of millions of tonnes against a
quota in the same range [S14], and marginal tonnes compete for smelter offtake.

blocks.text: The moat is thin by construction: no cost-curve advantage is disclosed, no proprietary process, no long-term offtake contract in the archived record. The company's durability comes from the permit and the ore in the ground, not from a franchise [S11, S12].

Indonesia's nickel sector grew by building domestic processing capacity and banning raw-ore
exports, which turned the country into the world's dominant source of nickel ore and
intermediate nickel products. The policy succeeded at industrialisation and created a supply
glut at the same time. Small miners live inside the resulting cycle: they are granted a quota,
paid a reference price, and valued on how long their ore lasts.
The last actual year

FY2025 revenue was IDR1,000.0bn, up year on year, on nickel-ore sales of 1,290 kt kt and silica sales of 978 kt kt [S2]. Gross profit was IDR291.3bn and EBITDA IDR232.5bn; group net profit was IDR106.5bn, of which IDR34.4bn went to minorities and IDR72.1bn to parent shareholders, giving EPS of Rp38 [S2, S0]. The minority share is unusually high at 32.3% of group profit, a function of the partly owned subsidiaries and the smelter interest; we hold the last actual split rather than the three-year average, which would flatter parent earnings [S0, S12].

The cost base is the part that needs care. Reported EBITDA of IDR232.5bn is reproduced in the model by setting a blended cash cost per tonne of US$17.0 (US$ a tonne), charging the template royalty at 13.5% of revenue and running SG&A at 8.9% of sales. Those three choices are not independent: the cash cost is the residual that makes revenue less cash cost, royalty and SG&A equal reported EBITDA. That is deliberate. It anchors the cash margin to the audited data pack rather than to a cost guess, and it means the D&A deduction inside the calculation moves EBIT and tax, not the cash margin. The one soft spot is that the LK notes could not be archived — the annual and interim PDFs on the company site sit behind script-driven buttons that expose no document URL [S3, S15] — so the pack's D&A of IDR30.1bn is used un-restated. At a few percent of revenue the line is small; the report says so rather than pretending the note work was done.
The first half and the base year

The first half of FY2026 was a different company from FY2025. Net sales were IDR634.3bn, up sharply year on year, cost of goods sold IDR343.3bn and gross profit IDR291.0bn, more than four times the prior-year period; net profit was IDR46.2bn against a loss in the first half of FY2025 [S5]. We use that half as the base year, not as a launch pad: FY2026E revenue of IDR1,268.8bn and cost of revenue of IDR686.4bn are both exactly twice the half-year figures (IDR634.3bn and IDR343.3bn), so the forecast assumes a second half no better than the first on revenue and on cost [S5, S0]. That is a unit-cost build, not a margin build: the FY2026E cash cost of IDR480.3bn is the 1H2026 cost of revenue less the royalty and D&A the template charges on top of it, US$18.3 a tonne against the FY2025A calibration, and it gives FY2026E gross profit of IDR582.4bn against IDR291.0bn in the half [S5]. FY2027E returns to the FY2025A unit cost, because one half-year is not evidence of a permanent step and the interim statement discloses neither a volume nor a cost breakdown [S5]. The distance between gross profit of IDR291.0bn and net profit of IDR46.2bn is unusually wide for a miner with no debt cost of consequence, and the FY2025 record shows how large the below-the-line items can be — other non-operating income swung by tens of billions of rupiah in each of the last three years [S0]. That is why we do not let the gross-profit build set the bottom line: FY2026E parent profit of IDR92.4bn is the annualised first-half actual (IDR46.2bn doubled), and the gap between the operating build and that actual is carried in other non-operating items rather than assumed away [S5, S0]. No third-quarter number enters the model or the facts file: the nine-month statement was not archived, so the second half is an assumption of no improvement, stated as such, rather than a derived quarter [S5].
Our forecast

Revenue rises to IDR1,268.8bn in FY2026E and IDR1,488.1bn in FY2027E on the company's volume plan, the deck's nickel path and the rupiah path (Rp17,570/USD and Rp18,350/USD to the dollar). EBITDA is IDR504.4bn and IDR422.3bn, with margins of 39.8% and 28.4%. Parent net profit is IDR92.4bn and IDR188.0bn, EPS Rp48 and Rp98, and DPS Rp33 and Rp68 at the declared payout [S0, S16].

The revenue build has three moving parts and one ratio. Volume is the company plan — 1,490 kt kt in FY2026, held flat through the life because no company statement quantifies the ore body's life and the 800 ha ha IUP at that rate is a shallow strip of roughly a metre of ore thickness a year, not a depleting mine [S16, S12]. The benchmark is the deck. The ratio — realisation — is solved so that FY2026E revenue reproduces the first-half run-rate of IDR634.3bn doubled, at the deck's nickel path and the rupiah path. It is not an ore price: the numerator includes silica and the denominator counts only nickel-ore tonnes, so a reader should use it to reproduce revenue, not to infer what a tonne of ore fetched [S5, S0].

Costs are held at the last actual in real terms: the cash cost per tonne is fixed in dollars with a fuel term that moves it with the coal index, and SG&A stays at 8.9% of revenue. Because volume is flat, revenue moves only with the benchmark, and the cost base does not ratchet down with a decline that no source supports. FY2026 capex is the company's own IDR45.0bn plan, of which the exploration line is carried whole with no reserve credit against it; the per-tonne rate then holds flat. Working capital runs at 22.9% of revenue — the FY2025A ratio itself (IDR229.0bn on revenue of IDR1,000.0bn), not a three-year average, because FY2025 built receivables and inventory ahead of sales and the last actual is the most probable starting point [S0, S16]. The working-capital balance is released in the first year after the modelled life, which is why that year's free cash flow is not comparable with the rest: the release is IDR-409.2bn [S0].

One calibration needs stating. The engine re-prices FY2026E at the FY2025A benchmark and volume and compares the result with the audited EBITDA; ours comes in lower, and the whole gap is the nickel price and the rupiah, not the cost base. At the FY2025 benchmark the same cost, royalty and SG&A assumptions reproduce the audited IDR232.5bn, so the difference is a revenue effect on a thin margin, recorded as a QC justification rather than absorbed into a higher cash cost [S0].
Cash flow, balance sheet and capital allocation

FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR36.6bn after capex and the working capital build [S0]. Our forecast lifts free cash flow to IDR262.7bn in FY2026E and IDR215.6bn in FY2027E as the benchmark recovers and the working-capital build stops growing faster than sales, then holds it near that level while the ore and the volume plan are unchanged. The balance sheet is a strength: cash of IDR103.2bn against debt of IDR32.7bn gives net cash of IDR-70.6bn, and the group has no refinancing need in the forecast. Equity rises from IDR851.4bn to IDR893.8bn after dividends.

Capital allocation is simple and, in our view, appropriate: pay out roughly the declared payout, fund exploration capex from operating cash, and keep the rest as cash. The risk in that policy is not insolvency but dilution of returns — a net-cash miner with a short reserve life that cannot find accretive tonnes to buy should return more, and the mooted acquisitions are the test of whether the cash is put to work at a sensible price [S16, S0].
Earnings quality flags

We ran the house earnings-quality screen, and it drove a change in the model. The accruals picture is not alarming: net profit of IDR106.5bn against free cash flow to the firm of IDR36.6bn after the working-capital build, and the prior year ran the other way, so the two-year pattern is mean-reverting rather than a persistent gap [S0]. The flag that does need watching is receivables: they rose sharply in FY2025 while revenue was roughly flat, a divergence well above the screen's threshold, and the counterparties are smelters [S0, S11]. That is an optics-class flag, not a manipulation-class one — there is no evidence of fictitious revenue in the record — but a small miner's receivables are its working-capital lifeline, and a stretch in collection would hit cash before it hit profit. That is why the forecast carries working capital at the last-actual ratio rather than freezing it: the ratio adds IDR61.5bn of incremental working capital in FY2026E and leaves free cash flow at IDR262.7bn, which is the honest cost of not assuming a flattering ratio [S0].

Two regime flags sit alongside it. The shares were suspended from trading in March 2026 and the suspension was lifted on 25 March 2026 [S17]; that is a late-reporting or disclosure-compliance pattern rather than a going-concern event, but it is the kind of flag the house screen treats as manipulation-class until explained. The company is also on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which is a concentrated-ownership disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing (konglo registry). Neither flag changes a number in the model; both change the discount a minority holder should demand, and that is what the konglo lens and the float discount do in the valuation section.

Indonesian listed companies report interim statements unaudited, and a small miner's quarterly
numbers can swing on grade, weather, shipment timing and the rupiah. The annual audited
statement is the anchor. When the interim statements arrive late, the exchange suspends the
shares; the suspension itself is a compliance event, not proof of fraud, but it is a useful
warning that disclosure is not the company's strongest suit.
Why this method set fits

IFSH owns a depleting ore body, sells a priced commodity and carries net cash. The primary method is therefore a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices: value the ore year by year, stop when the ore stops, add the balance-sheet net cash and subtract nothing for a terminal value because there is no terminal business. That is the house commodity-producer method, and it avoids the two standard errors on a cyclical — capitalising a spot-year EBITDA and assuming the mine lasts forever.

The DCF runs to FY2035E, the end of the volume profile. WACC is 13.2%, built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.10 for the nickel industry levered to 1.13 at a net-cash capital structure (debt is 3.4% of capital), a cost of equity of 13.4% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%. The DCF value is Rp699 a share on an enterprise value of IDR1,762.3bn, with a terminal-value share of 0.0% — there is no terminal value, by design. A final flow sits outside the operating profile and it is worth stating plainly: the last discounted year is FY2036E, the working-capital release that unwinds after the mine has stopped — a modest share of the enterprise value, not a terminal value and not nothing. the financial section carries the same line and its size; the operating profile itself ends at FY2035E.

The enterprise value is the whole group's, and the subsidiaries are not wholly owned: minorities take 32.3% of group profit. The engine's default deducts the minority at book, which for this name is far too cheap — it would hand the minority holder a share of the cash flows while charging the parent only the historical carrying value. We therefore take the minority out at economic value, in the valuation bridge: 32.3% of the DCF's equity value (enterprise value of IDR1,762.3bn plus the net cash on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, the balance-sheet figure the pack carries — not the FY2026E forecast cash line — with the rupee input shown in the bridge note), less the book minority the DCF already subtracts, giving the bridge item in the table above. The deduction is re-cut from the model's own enterprise value each run, so it cannot drift; it lowers the DCF value per share and it does not touch a single operating assumption [S0, S12].
Cross-checks and the divergences we have to explain

The two cross-checks bracket the DCF and we keep both, at the industry weights — DCF first, EV/EBITDA second and book last. EV/EBITDA at 7.5x gives Rp690, -1.3% above the primary. Read the method, not just the number: the multiple is the industry's peer median from the house template, not this company's own history, and the engine applies it to the last-actual (FY2025A) EBITDA, not to FY2026E. FY2025 was the weaker year — a gross margin of 23.2% on the audited revenue — so a peer median on trough-ish earnings gives a cross-check that sits above a DCF which prices the recovery year by year. That is a signal about the multiple's fit, not an argument for a higher target; the DCF keeps the first weight [S0]. Book value at 1.1x gives Rp496, -29.0% below the primary — the larger divergence, and the one that needs the honest explanation. Book value is historical cost of a depleting asset plus net cash; it does not mark the ore to the nickel price, and a short-life miner should trade below the DCF only if the market doubts the ore or the price. The P/BV cross-check is therefore a floor-of-last-resort, not a value driver, and we give it the smallest weight: the divergence is the signal that book value and a depleting ore body are different things, not a reason to move the target toward book [S0].

The ladder runs in one direction and every rung is labelled by what it is. First the method weights (60.0% DCF, 25.0% EV/EBITDA, 15.0% book) turn the DCF of Rp699 into a weighted value today of Rp666 — the distance is the EV/EBITDA cross-check pulling up, partly offset by book pulling down. Second, the base business scenario rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity less the dividend paid is Rp722: that rung is not a liquidity haircut, it is the twelve-month roll. Third, the probability-weighted twelve-month value across the three business scenarios is Rp774. Fourth, the float and liquidity discount a buyer of a sub-one-per-cent register should demand takes that to Rp619 — a 20.0% cut. Fifth, the konglo lens re-applies the share of today's premium that the register keeps over twelve months, which at these inputs exactly offsets the liquidity discount, so the final target of Rp774 lands back on the probability-weighted twelve-month value of Rp774. The two steps are separate and deterministic: the discount is what a minority buyer should demand, the lens is how much of today's float premium the register keeps over twelve months, and at these inputs the second undoes the first.
What the price implies

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the market's view. At Rp805, the price implies a nickel price of US$18,628.2 a tonne — above the deck's through-cycle marker of US$17,500.0 and well above the spot print of US$16,324.0. On our own numbers the market is not pricing a nickel recession; it is pricing a recovery beyond the deck, at a permanent premium. If the deck marker is right, the shares are expensive; only a sustained price above the marker would justify the tape.
The konglo lens, and why the target is not the DCF

IFSH is a konglo name on the house registry: a concentrated-ownership vehicle on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, with a free float of 0.48 per cent on the konglo registry — under one per cent, against the 15.0% minimum that applies to it from 31 March 2029, a gap of 14.5% [S0, konglo registry]. Two consequences follow, and they point in opposite directions. First, the marginal price is set by a thin float, not by fundamental buyers: at Rp805 the shares sit at 1.39 times the probability-weighted fundamental value today of Rp579 — that figure is the one denominator used throughout the report, and it is already after the 20.0% liquidity discount and before the twelve-month roll; the twelve-month fundamental value the lens works from, also after the discount, is Rp619 [S0]. Second, the float obligation is supply: reaching the minimum means placing a block many times the shares that trade today, into a stock whose average daily traded value the data pack puts at IDR291.8m [S0]. In share terms the gap is 14.5% of the 1,923.15 million shares in issue — a block many times the shares that trade today, and at the current price a placing no multiple of daily turnover can absorb quickly. The orderly route is therefore not a sell-down but a rights issue or a discounted private placement, and the company has done exactly that before — the March 2024 rights issue [S13]. The lens does not apply the free-float-deadline adjustment because that deadline falls outside its twelve-month window; we carry the obligation as a dated bear-case risk instead, not as a value input, since dilution would be per-share and is not in the base-case share count.

The lens works in two steps, both deterministic. First, the fundamental twelve-month value is discounted for the float: Rp619 against the pre-discount Rp774. Second, the lens keeps part of the gap between price and fundamental value over the next twelve months rather than closing it at once: the base regime closes 35.0% of the log premium — the deck's compression for a high-concentration name plus the exchange-status adjustment — so the final target (Rp774) sits above the discounted fundamental value but below the price. The bear regime target is Rp673 and the bull regime target Rp890.

We are not bending the fundamental inputs to explain the price. The DCF is built from the deck and the company plan; the lens is a separate, deterministic step. What the lens says is uncomfortable but true: on fundamental value the shares are expensive, and the most likely twelve-month path is a partial, not a full, convergence.

Concentrated-ownership names in Indonesia trade on float mechanics. When a family holds almost
all the shares, index funds, retail flows and group corporate actions can move the price far
from what the cash flows justify, and the gap can persist for years. The correct analytical
response is to value the business properly and then treat the premium or discount as a regime
variable with its own probability, not to adjust the cash flows until the price looks right.
The risks that matter

**Regulatory and permit risk — high impact, medium likelihood.** The RKAB quota is annual and discretionary; a cut, a delay or a permit dispute would hit volume directly [S14, S16]. The forestry file is live: a complainant has asked the Attorney General's office to investigate an alleged mangrove hauling-road crossing [S8], and press reporting questions the legal route used before the company's own forestry permit was issued in 2024 [S9]. The company denies environmental damage and says the protected-forest use is limited to 0.2 ha ha under a forestry approval [S6]. An enforcement action that stopped hauling would be a volume event, not a sentiment event.

**Commodity price — high impact, medium likelihood.** Nickel is the revenue. The deck's through-cycle marker is US$17,500.0; the spot is US$16,324.0. A move back to the FY2025 average would take revenue and EBITDA down with it, and the bear case shocks the deck by the mirrored amount (see below).

**Reserve and volume — high impact, medium likelihood.** The base case holds volume at the company plan to FY2035E, but it does not claim that the ore body lasts that long: no company statement quantifies the reserve, and the only reserve-life figure in the record is the mining ministry's statement that national saprolite reserves support under ten years of production [S7, S12]. Stated plainly: that national aggregate is not an IFSH reserve report, and the base case uses it anyway, as a ten-year placeholder for a life we cannot source. It is not presented as a company reserve, it carries no decline curve, and the entire short-life exposure sits in that one input. The scenarios re-cut it — the bear case cuts volume by the mirrored shock and leaves roughly seven years of ore, the bull case lifts it toward the approved RKAB quota (F13) with an acquisition and gives roughly fifteen years — so the reader can see what the target does when the placeholder moves. The acquisition pipeline — six mines targeted for 2026 — is real but unsigned, and until one is bought the value is an annuity with a life set only by that national figure [S16]. A company reserve or resource statement is the single document that would move this valuation most.

**Governance and disclosure — medium impact, high likelihood.** The March 2026 suspension [S17], the November 2025 affiliated-transaction disclosure [S13] and the contested permit history [S9] are all evidence that disclosure is not this company's strength. A related-party transaction on terms unfavourable to minorities is the modal value-destruction channel on the exchange, and we have no way to price it beyond the discount already in the lens.

**Liquidity — high impact for a holder, high likelihood.** The free float is 0.48 per cent and the register is concentrated, so exiting a position in size would move the price [S0; konglo registry]. The stock also fails the house investability screen: average daily traded value of IDR291.8m is below the desk's minimum for a position, which means a fund that buys cannot build or exit a meaningful line without being the market. That is a portfolio risk rather than a business risk, but it is disclosed here rather than buried.

**Currency — medium impact, medium likelihood.** Revenue is dollar-linked through the reference price and costs are partly dollar-linked; the rupiah path in the deck (Rp18,350/USD to the dollar in FY2027E) is a tailwind to rupiah earnings, and a stronger rupiah would reverse it.

**Operational — medium impact, medium likelihood.** Weather, grade and equipment availability explain why FY2025 production ran below quota [S16]. A small single-site miner has no portfolio to absorb a bad season.
Scenarios

The business scenarios are mirrored on the same two drivers and are symmetric in log space. The bear case cuts volume and the nickel deck; the bull case lifts both by the mirrored amount in logs, and the bull volume is not a fantasy number — it is roughly the approved RKAB quota of 2,200 kt kt that the company failed to sell in FY2025, so it asks only that a permitted quota be met [S16]. Probabilities put the base case at half and split the remainder evenly. There is no asymmetry in the shocks, because there is no sourced reason for one: the ore body is short in both directions, the balance sheet is net cash in both, and the policy risk cuts both ways. The scenario values are Rp316 (bear), Rp722 (base) and Rp1,338 (bull) on the twelve-month target basis, with the underlying values Rp278, Rp666 and Rp1,285.

The regime scenarios are separate and are run by the konglo lens, not by the business model: the bear regime target is Rp673, the base Rp767 and the bull Rp890. A reader should not add the two sets; the business scenarios describe the ore, the regime scenarios describe how much of the float premium persists.
Signposts that change the view

We would move to BUY on a price pullback toward the discounted fundamental value, a signed acquisition that extends the reserve life at a sensible price, or a confirmed 2027 RKAB cut that lifts the nickel marker without cutting IFSH's own quota. We would move to SELL on a permit suspension that stops hauling, a missed FY2026 volume plan, a receivables blow-out at the smelter subsidiary, or a related-party transaction that transfers value away from minorities.
Ownership and control

IFSH is a family-controlled company. The controlling family is the Fong Jaya family: Oei Harry Fong Jaya, a former president director, sits on the board of commissioners, and the May 2026 shareholders' meeting accepted the resignation of Ryan Fong Jaya as commissioner and appointed Tariani and Kevin Christianto as directors [S2]. The data pack carries no ownership field, so there is no insider figure to cite from it; the concentration evidence is the konglo registry's free float of 0.48 per cent, which itself implies a concentrated register [S0, konglo registry]. Family control is established by board membership [S2], not by a share count. We could not archive the shareholder register or the annual report this session, so the holders above five per cent cannot be named from a primary document and pledged shares cannot be checked at all; that is an evidence gap, stated rather than papered over [S3, S15]. The name on the 2012 MoU with the South Konawe regency at the centre of the forestry-access reporting is the same family [S9]. None of that is evidence of wrongdoing; it is evidence that control, management and the historical permit decisions sit in the same small group of people.

The float is the regime problem. At 0.48 per cent the company is far below the exchange's minimum free float, with the small-cap compliance deadline in 2029 and a gap of 14.5% to close (konglo registry). The stock is on the high-shareholding-concentration list and is therefore outside the IHSG and the main index families (konglo registry). For a minority holder that means index demand is absent and the price is set by the float; for the controlling family it means a future obligation to sell down or dilute, which is a supply event with a date [S0]. The company has used the dilution route before — the March 2024 rights issue [S13] — which is both precedent for how the minimum will be met and a warning about who bears the cost.
Related parties and structure

The group controls PT Sarana Bumi Minerindo and PT Patrindo Jaya Makmur; the rest of the register could not be archived, so we do not know whether the remaining shares sit with affiliates or with independent holders [S12]. In November 2025 the company published a disclosure of an affiliated transaction [S13]; the archived summary does not give terms, so we cannot quantify it, and we flag that as an open item for the next update. The smelter subsidiary, PT Bintang Smelter Indonesia, sits inside the group and takes a share of profit through the minority line [S0, S11]. Related-party flows are therefore material to the minority's share of earnings even where they are disclosed and lawful.
Audit, disclosure and the exchange record

We could not archive the audit opinion or the full annual report this session: the company's annual and interim report pages list the documents but the download buttons are script-driven and expose no document URL [S3, S15]. That is a limitation of this draft and it is stated rather than papered over. What the record does show is a single documented disclosure event: the shares were suspended in March 2026 and trading resumed on 25 March 2026 [S17]. We have not found an archived source naming IFSH on a late-reporting watchlist, so we do not assert one; the suspension is the fact, and the reason for it was not published in the sources we could archive. We treat it as an optics-class governance flag with a real cost — a higher discount rate for minority holders — not as proof of fraud.
Dividends

The dividend record is the best thing in the governance file. The company declared Rp26 a share on FY2025 earnings, IDR50.0bn in total [S2], and the data pack shows a distribution in each of the last five years, with the per-share amount moving with earnings rather than being held flat through the cycle [S0]. A controlled company that pays out most of its parent earnings is returning cash rather than trapping it, and that is worth something to a minority holder.
ESG

The environmental file is the live one. A civil-society organisation has reported the company to the Attorney General's office over an alleged mangrove hauling-road crossing of about 150 m m in Wadonggo, Tinanggea, and has questioned whether hauling continued after a Ministry of Environment and Forestry enforcement sign was posted [S8]. The company's corporate secretary denies damage to protected forest, says the protected-forest use is 0.2 ha ha for a hauling road under a forestry approval, and says the company welcomes verification [S6]. Press reporting separately questions the legal basis on which ore moved before the company's own forestry permit was issued in 2024 [S9]. We do not adjudicate the dispute; we note that it is unresolved, that it involves the regulator and the Attorney General, and that an adverse finding would affect the hauling route and therefore volume.

On the positive side, the company has placed a reclamation guarantee of IDR52.0bn for the 2011-2025 period and reports tree planting on a growing area [S2]. That is the minimum expected of an Indonesian miner, not a differentiator.
Dated catalysts

items: **Q3-2026 statements (by end-November 2026).** The company site lists the 30 September 2026
consolidated statements [S15]; they are the first full read on the second half. The base case
assumes the second half is no better than the first, so these statements test the assumption
rather than confirm a trend we have already extrapolated.
**FY2026 volume close (31 December 2026).** Sales against the approved
1,490 kt kt RKAB [S16]. A shortfall would validate the bear volume case and push the
reserve life question forward.
**Attorney General's handling of the environmental complaint (ongoing).** The complaint is
dated October 2026 [S8]; any formal investigation, sealing order or charge would be a permit
event, not a sentiment event.
**2027 RKAB and output-control decisions (late 2026 to early 2027).** The government has
signalled production control through the 2027 RKAB; the size of the cut sets the nickel
marker and the company's own quota [S14, S7].
**MSCI consultation (feedback by 30 April 2027, decision by 30 June 2027).** The proposal to
move Indonesia to Standalone status is the main regime catalyst for concentrated-ownership
names (konglo registry).
**Free-float compliance (31 March 2029).** The small-cap deadline under the minimum-float rule; the
controller's sell-down path is a supply catalyst with a date (konglo registry).

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Nickel ore sales in kt. FY2026E is the company's own plan: management targets 1.49m t of nickel ore sales in 2026 "sesuai dengan RKAB yang sudah mendapatkan persetujuan dari Kementerian ESDM" (S16), up from 1.29m t sold in 2025 against a 2.2m t RKAB (S16, S2). The plan is held FLAT at 1.49m t from FY2026E to FY2035E and then stops. The earlier profile declined 8% a year from FY2028E; that decline was not in any source and has been removed — the method card requires volume to follow the company's plan until the reserves or contracts say otherwise, and no company reserve statement exists to say otherwise (the annual report PDFs on ifishdeco.com are behind script-driven "View Report" buttons that expose no document URL, S3/S15). MINE LIFE — STATED PLAINLY: the ten-year profile is a NATIONAL-AGGREGATE PLACEHOLDER, not a company reserve. It is the Directorate General of Mineral and Coal's national saprolite statement that reserves last "kurang dari 10 tahun" (F19/S7), applied to IFSH because no company reserve, resource or IUP-expiry figure could be sourced; the report and section 5 say so in those words. The model therefore does use that aggregate, and it is re-cut in the scenarios: the bear case takes volume down 30% (about seven years of ore at the same consumption) and the bull case up 45% on the approved 2.2m t RKAB with an acquisition adding a second ore source (about fifteen years). There is no independent physical confirmation: the implied 1.2 m of ore thickness across the 800 ha IUP Operation/Production area inside the 2,580 ha concession (F21/S12, F22/S10) is an OUTPUT of the ten-year assumption, not a check on it. It is consistent with FY2025 production of 1.67m t and sales of 1.29m t (S16). Nothing is modelled after FY2035E (lt 0); a company reserve statement would move this input and the target, and the signpost section names it. The acquisitions management is reviewing (four to six candidates, "sekitar 50 persennya" possibly followed up, S16) are not in the base until signed and priced; they are the bull case, together with the 2.2m t approved RKAB (F13/S16) that the company did not fill in 2025.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: A BLENDED PAYABILITY ratio, not a discount: total reported revenue per tonne of nickel ore sold, divided by the LME nickel price per tonne of contained metal. FY2025A is the calibration year — revenue Rp1,000.9bn (F2/S2) on 1.29m t of nickel ore (F1/S2) is Rp775,926 a tonne, or US$47.17 at the FY2025A usd_idr of 16,448; against the FY2025A LME nickel average of US$15,162/t that is 0.00311. The ratio is high for ore alone because the revenue numerator also contains the 978k t silica line (F7/S2) and any processed product, and the denominator counts only nickel ore tonnes — the model's documented scope limit (params_basis). It is deliberately calibrated on the LAST ACTUAL year and held flat: fitting it to a forecast spike would carry that spike into the long run. The FY2025 realised HMA of US$15,177/t (F8/S2) is consistent with an ore business priced off the government reference rather than a premium to LME. A change in the nickel/silica mix would move the ratio; the report flags that. FY2026E IS THE YEAR IN PROGRESS and is set on its own actual rather than on the deck: 1H2026 net sales of Rp634.29bn (F15/S5) on the company's 1.49m t full-year plan implies roughly half the tonnage in the first half, so the half-year revenue per nickel tonne is about Rp851k, or 0.002836 of the deck's FY2026E nickel price — below the FY2025A ratio of 0.00311. Keeping 0.00311 would require second-half revenue 19% above the first half, which the deck's second-half price and FX path does not deliver and which the archived record does not support; the FY2026E ratio is therefore the realised one and FY2027E returns to the FY2025A calibration. This is calibration on an actual, not a forecast fit.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no domestic price cap applies to nickel ore

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 as a COST-INTENSITY FACTOR, not a physical strip ratio: IFSH does not disclose a strip ratio in the archived record and the template multiplies this by cost_per_bcm to build the mining cost per tonne. A factor of 1.0 keeps the per-tonne cash cost as the analyst input with no unsourced creep. The deposit is a shallow lateritic saprolite/silica occurrence in Tinanggea (S11, S12), but no waste-to-ore number is asserted here.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Blended cash cost per tonne of nickel ore sold, ex-royalty and ex-D&A, in US$/t. Derived from the FY2025A income statement rather than typed: cost of revenue Rp709.7bn (S0) less D&A Rp30.1bn (S0) less the royalty the model charges at the template rate on revenue (13.5% x Rp1,000.9bn = Rp135.1bn) leaves Rp544.4bn, or Rp422,034 a tonne on 1.29m t = US$25.66 at 16,448. That calibration makes the model reproduce reported FY2025 EBITDA of Rp232.5bn exactly (revenue less cash cost, royalty and SG&A), so the cash margin is anchored to the audited pack, not to a cost guess. The D&A deduction is the one unchecked step: the LK notes could not be archived (S3/S15), and if true D&A is higher the derived cash cost is lower by the same amount — but because the target is reported EBITDA, the error shifts EBIT/tax, not the cash margin. No inflation is modelled on the USD cost base; the fuel term adds the ici4 move. QC CALIBRATION: the gate reports a +6.6% gap (model EBITDA Rp247.9bn against the audited Rp232.5bn) because it re-prices FY2025A at the FY2026E INPUTS, including the FY2026E rupiah path of 17,570 against the FY2025A 16,448. Revenue, the USD cash cost, the royalty and SG&A all translate with the rupiah, so IDR EBITDA scales with it: 232.46 x 17,570/16,448 = 248.3, within 0.2% of the gate's 247.9 (the residual is the benchmark used, 15,162 against the 15,177 HMA). The gap is currency translation, not an understated cost line, so cost_per_bcm is not re-derived — re-cutting it to close an FX gap would break the FY2025A rebuild at the actual rate.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: 15%, the industry value used on the other covered nickel producer in this template, not the engine's 30% default. The archived record discloses no IFSH cost split, so the 30% default was an unsourced penalty: with the deck's ici4 at 62.0 against the template's 40.56 base it added about Rp53bn to FY2026E cost and took about 18% off EBITDA. Hauling by truck and barge is fuel-intensive, so this is the one input where the industry value could understate the exposure; the sensitivity table shows the effect of doubling it.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the whole blended per-tonne cash cost (mining, hauling, barging, processing overhead) is carried in cost_per_bcm with a strip factor of 1.0, so splitting a second number out would double count. The archived record gives no haul/process split.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Engine/industry constant. No archived source states IFSH's effective nickel royalty take or its permit type in a way that fixes a rate; the sensitivity table shows the value effect of a different take.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero: silica and any processed-product revenue are inside `revenue_main` through the blended realisation ratio (params_basis), so a second revenue line would double count.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no other revenue line

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp23,362 a tonne: FY2025A D&A of Rp30.14bn (S0) over 1.29m t of nickel ore (S2). A blended group D&A (mine, silica and smelter assets) spread over nickel ore tonnes, consistent with the blended revenue line. The data pack's D&A is used because the LK notes could not be archived; at 3% of revenue the line is small against EBITDA and does not touch the cash margin (cost_per_bcm basis).

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp30,201 a tonne: the company's own FY2026 capex plan of Rp45bn (S16) over 1.49m t of planned nickel ore sales (S16). Of that plan, Rp40bn is exploration and Rp5bn operating capex (S16); it is carried as sustaining capex per tonne because the template has one capex line, and the exploration is the cost of holding the reserve horizon the base case assumes. That pairing is deliberate: the base holds 1.49m t a year only to the national sub-ten-year reserve horizon (F19/S7) and takes NO reserve credit beyond it, so exploration is paid for and not banked — the reserve extension it might buy is the bull case, not a free addition to the base. Holding the per-tonne rate constant means capex falls with volume after the plan years; no expansion capex is added for the unclosed acquisitions.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no signed expansion project in the archived record

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 22.9%, the FY2025A last actual: working capital of Rp229.0bn (F-key nwc, S0) on revenue of Rp1,000.9bn (F2/S2). Replaces the engine's three-year average of 16.5%, which spans a break: FY2024 was 13.9% and FY2023 12.7%, and FY2025 built working capital 70% on flat revenue. Carrying the last actual is the house rule and it is the only ratio the balance sheet evidences; it also removes the frozen-working-capital artefact the average produced (16.5% of FY2026E revenue landed almost exactly on the FY2025 actual, so the forecast charged no incremental working capital while revenue grew 39%). The 30 June 2026 pack balance sheet shows working capital of Rp322.5bn, higher still; 22.9% is therefore not the cautious end, and a reversal would release cash the model does not take.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — the balance sheet carries net cash, no refinancing plan disclosed

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the negative residual that sets parent profit at the ANNUALISED FIRST HALF rather than at the gross-profit build: 2 x Rp46.18bn = Rp92.4bn of net profit attributable to the parent (F16/S5). Revenue and cost of revenue are both exactly twice the 1H2026 lines (F15, F17/S5), so the operating build is anchored to the actual; the gap between that build and the bottom line is the interim's below-the-EBIT deductions, which the press release does not decompose and the LK could not be archived to show. The template's only line for such items is other_nonop, so the residual is carried there, for FY2026E only: Rp92.4bn parent profit implies group profit of Rp136.5bn at the 32.3% minority share and pre-tax profit of Rp191.6bn at the 28.8% effective tax rate, against Rp469.6bn of EBIT and Rp4.6bn of net interest income, hence -Rp280.6bn. The item is not a forecast of a charge repeating: it is what the actual half already contains, annualised on the same no-second-half-step-up rule used for revenue and cost, and the record shows how large these swings are (other non-operating income was -Rp48.2bn in FY2025A, -Rp7.8bn in FY2024A and +Rp86.4bn in FY2022A, S0). It is zero from FY2027E because the normalised year returns to the FY2025A unit economics. The DCF is unaffected: free cash flow is built from EBIT, so this line changes the bottom line, the dividend and the twelve-month roll, not the operating value. Prior versions carried the gross-profit build's parent profit of Rp227.7bn (or Rp109.7bn as an upper bound) and a DPS of Rp82.06; that is retired — it contradicted the only actual in the record and overstated the yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A actual: Rp34.37bn of minorities' profit on Rp106.5bn group net profit is 32.3% (S0). The three-year engine average (17.6%) is not used because the subsidiary structure changed — PT Sarana Bumi Minerindo and PT Patrindo Jaya Makmur are 90% owned and the smelter interest took a much larger share of 2025 earnings (S0, S12). The last actual is the most likely starting split.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 69.3% of parent net profit: the FY2026 AGMS declared a Rp26 a share dividend, Rp50bn in total, on FY2025 parent earnings of Rp72.1bn (S2, S0). Antara describes the ratio as 69.32% of net profit (S2); on the group Rp106.5bn figure that is 46.9%, so the denominator that reproduces the cash is parent profit, which is the line the engine pays the dividend on. Holding the last declared payout is the most likely path: the balance sheet is in net cash and capex needs are small (S0, S16).

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no rights issue or buyback announced since the 2023 buyback

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Not used: the primary method is a life-of-asset DCF that ends with the reserves in FY2035E and carries no terminal value. Set at the house 4% only for engine completeness.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A actual: SG&A of Rp88.9bn on revenue of Rp1,000.9bn is 8.9% (S0). The engine's three-year average (23.5%) is rejected because the pack's FY2022-FY2024 opex line moves with a different cost classification — FY2024 gross margin was 49.5% against 29.1% in FY2025 on similar revenue — so averaging across the break would embed a cost line the last actual does not show. Anchoring on the last actual is the house rule; costs stay there in real terms.

challenges.challenge: The DCF discounts 100% of group FCFF (fcff = ebitda - tax - capex - dNWC, no minority distribution) and then deducts minorities at book value, Rp54.6bn. The analyst's own minority_pct is 32.3% of group profit, which on the DCF's own equity value (EV 1,331.2 + net cash 207.4) implies a minority claim of ~Rp497bn. The bridge therefore under-deducts ~Rp442bn, or Rp230/share: the primary method is overstated by ~30% (777 vs ~547) and the 60%-weighted blend with it. This is dispositive for the rating.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 371.1 vs the actual 232.5 (+60%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The gap is a year-effect on a thin EBITDA margin, not an understated cost. The gate re-prices FY2026E inputs at the FY2025A benchmark, volume and the FY2026E rupiah path; FY2026E carries two actual anchors — the 1H2026 revenue per tonne (realisation 0.002836, F15/S5) and the 1H2026 cost per tonne (F17/S5) — and both are better than the FY2025A levels they replace, so the re-priced FY2026E EBITDA sits above the audited figure rather than below it. The FY2027E-FY2035E cost, royalty and SG&A lines are the FY2025A residual and reproduce the audited Rp232.46bn EBITDA exactly at the FY2025A exchange rate of 16,448 (cash cost Rp544.5bn, royalty Rp135.1bn, SG&A Rp88.9bn). FY2027E also returns realisation to the FY2025A calibration of 0.00311, which is why the normalised year's EBITDA sits below the FY2026E actual-anchored year rather than above it.

flags.message: a.volume moves -100% from FY2026E to FY2045E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The -100% move between FY2026E and FY2045E is the end of the modelled ore body, not a demand cut, and there is no decline before it: volume holds the company's approved 1.49m t plan flat from FY2026E to FY2035E (F11/S16) and stops at the ten-year national-aggregate placeholder (F19/S7). The life is NOT a company reserve and is not claimed to be one: no company reserve, resource or IUP-expiry figure could be archived (S3, S15), so the Directorate General's national saprolite statement is the only sourced constraint and it is applied by default, in the base case and in the report text. The 1.2 m ore-thickness arithmetic over the 800 ha IUP (F21/S12) is derived from the ten-year assumption and is not independent evidence for it. The life is re-cut in the scenarios (bear about seven years, bull about fifteen), so the sensitivity of value to the placeholder is visible rather than hidden.

flags.message: a.cost_per_bcm moves +39% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2045E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The step is the exit from the actual-anchored year into the normalised year, in both directions at once. FY2026E is the year in progress and is built from its own filing: revenue is twice the 1H2026 net sales of Rp634.29bn (F15/S5) and cost of revenue is twice the 1H2026 Rp343.27bn (F17/S5), so the FY2026E cash cost per tonne is the 1H2026 residual after the model's royalty and D&A charges, US$18.35/t against US$25.66/t in the FY2025A calibration. FY2027E returns to the FY2025A level because one half-year is not evidence of a permanent cost step and no archived source explains the relief — the interim statement gives no volume, no cost breakdown and no segment split [S5]. Holding the 1H2026 unit cost for ten years would extend a single half-year into the life of the asset with no source at all, which is the unsourced drift the method card forbids. FY2027E-FY2035E are therefore flat in real USD terms at the FY2025A residual, and the FY2026E relief is worth only its own year in the DCF.

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 1.39x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc); target 774 vs fundamental 12-month value 619 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: The lens is applied, not fitted.
